content: In many countries, second-generation antipsychotic drugs, also known as atypical antipsychotics, are the first-line treatment for individuals with schizophrenia. However, the comparative effects of these drugs remain unclear. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of quetiapine in comparison to other second-generation antipsychotics for the treatment of schizophrenia and related psychoses. The researchers conducted a systematic search of the Cochrane Schizophrenia Group Trials Register (as of May 2010), reviewed references from identified studies, and contacted pharmaceutical companies, drug approval agencies, and trial authors for additional information. They included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared oral quetiapine with other oral atypical antipsychotics in individuals with schizophrenia or schizophrenia-like psychoses. Data were independently extracted. For dichotomous outcomes, risk ratios (RRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated using an intention-to-treat approach with a random-effects model. For continuous outcomes, mean differences (MDs) were calculated using the same model. The number needed to treat for an additional beneficial outcome (NNTB) was also determined when appropriate. The efficacy data generally favored the comparator drugs over quetiapine. For example, when compared to olanzapine, quetiapine was associated with a higher Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS) total score (11 RCTs, n = 1486; mean quetiapine endpoint score 3.67 higher; CI 1.95 to 5.39; low quality). Similarly, quetiapine had a higher PANSS score compared to risperidone (13 RCTs, n = 2155; mean quetiapine endpoint score 1.74 higher; CI 0.19 to 3.29; moderate quality) and paliperidone (1 RCT, n = 319; mean quetiapine endpoint score 6.30 higher; CI 2.77 to 9.83; moderate quality). However, the clinical significance of these differences remains unclear. No significant differences in mental state outcomes were observed when quetiapine was compared to clozapine, aripiprazole, or ziprasidone. Quetiapine was associated with fewer movement disorders compared to olanzapine (7 RCTs, n = 1127; RR for use of antiparkinson medication 0.51; CI 0.32 to 0.81; moderate quality) and less weight gain (8 RCTs, n = 1667; RR 0.68; CI 0.51 to 0.92; moderate quality) and glucose elevation. However, quetiapine was linked to an increased risk of QTc prolongation (3 RCTs, n = 643; MD 4.81; CI 0.34 to 9.28). When compared to risperidone, quetiapine caused fewer movement disorders (8 RCTs, n = 2163; RR for use of antiparkinson medication 0.50; CI 0.36 to 0.69; moderate quality) and less prolactin elevation (7 RCTs, n = 1733; MD -35.25; CI -43.59 to -26.91). However, quetiapine was associated with a greater increase in cholesterol levels (6 RCTs, n = 1473; MD 8.57; CI 4.85 to 12.29). Limited data suggest that quetiapine caused fewer parkinsonian side effects compared to paliperidone (1 RCT, n = 319; RR for use of antiparkinson medication 0.64; CI 0.45 to 0.91; moderate quality), less prolactin elevation (1 RCT, n = 319; MD -49.30; CI -57.80 to -40.80), and less weight gain (1 RCT, n = 319; RR for weight gain of 7% or more of total body weight 2.52; CI 0.50 to 12.78; moderate quality). Compared to ziprasidone, quetiapine caused fewer extrapyramidal side effects (1 RCT, n = 522; RR for use of antiparkinson medication 0.43; CI 0.20 to 0.93; moderate quality) and less prolactin elevation. However, quetiapine was more sedating and caused greater weight gain (2 RCTs, n = 754; RR 2.22; CI 1.35 to 3.63; moderate quality) and cholesterol elevation. The authors concluded that most individuals who start quetiapine discontinue it within a few weeks, with approximately 60% stopping treatment. There is no available data comparing quetiapine to amisulpride, sertindole, or zotepine. While efficacy data favor olanzapine and risperidone over quetiapine, the clinical relevance of these findings is uncertain. Quetiapine may cause fewer parkinsonian side effects compared to paliperidone, aripiprazole, ziprasidone, risperidone, and olanzapine. Its weight gain profile appears similar to risperidone, clozapine, and aripiprazole, though data for the latter two are limited. Quetiapine may cause more weight gain than ziprasidone but less than olanzapine and paliperidone. The available data are limited by assumptions and biases, highlighting the need for further research into the effects of quetiapine.
